comments.author: tom@lant.uk
comments.text:
Good instinct to flag this. Based on how these proxies (jira-proxy.js, salesforce-proxy.js) are written, there are two concrete gaps
    relative to what you're hoping is already true:

    1. They're not actually localhost-only right now. They're started with http.createServer(...).listen(PORT, callback) — no host argument.
       Node's default when you omit the host is to bind 0.0.0.0, i.e. all network interfaces, not just the loopback interface. So as
       written, anything else on your LAN that can reach your machine's IP on that port could hit it — this isn't just a "hopefully"
       situation, it's actually open beyond localhost today. The fix is to pass the host explicitly: .listen(PORT, '127.0.0.1', callback).
    2. CORS is wide open: both set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, meaning any page loaded in the same browser — not just wigwag.html — can
       make a cross-origin fetch to http://localhost:8934/:8936 and pull data through it, if it can guess the endpoint shape (which isn't
       secret — it's public in this repo). That's a real vector even with correct localhost-only binding, since a malicious or compromised
       tab running in your own browser is still "local" from the proxy's point of view.

    Beyond fixing #1, a few things worth layering on:

    - Tighten CORS to the actual origin wigwag is served from instead of * — trickier if you open wigwag.html via file:// (origin comes
      through as null), but still narrows the surface for the common case of serving it over http.
    - A shared-secret header: have wigwag's Settings hold a token that gets sent on every proxy request, and have the proxy reject anything
      without it. This is the strongest single addition, because it defends against the "other local process/rogue tab" case that
      localhost-only binding alone doesn't cover — binding restricts network origin, not same-machine origin.
    - Minimize the exposure window: only run the proxy while you're actually linking things, then kill it, rather than leaving it up
      indefinitely.
    - One thing already done reasonably well: the startup/status logging only ever prints the auth mode (token / password-flow), never the
      actual credentials or fetched record contents — so at least nothing sensitive is landing in a terminal scrollback or log file by
      default.

    The localhost-binding fix (#1) is the one I'd treat as not-optional — it's a real, currently-open gap, not a hypothetical one.

history.text: Description set to "Right now a repo nothing can read just leaves the Connect b…"
history.value: Right now a repo nothing can read just leaves the Connect button disabled in Connect Remote's probe sheet -- no explanation why, no next step. The remotes.zip design handoff's own 13c frame specifies a richer screen: per-identity failure reasons surfaced individually (expired token vs. never had access vs. repo doesn't exist -- probeGithubRepoAccess already returns a reason field for this, just unused downstream), a Re-authorize action for an expired token, a Request access action (needs its own design pass, nothing in this codebase sends outbound requests to a repo owner today), and reusing a credential that's already proven itself against a different remote (not designed in the source material either).

history.text: Title set to "First write on a read-only-connected project"
history.value: First write on a read-only-connected project

history.text: Description set to "A project connected as public-read-only (or via a single id…"
history.value: A project connected as public-read-only (or via a single identity that can read but not write) has no path today from having it open to actually changing something. The remotes.zip handoff frames this as an evolution of the existing first-write attribution gate (requireAttribution) rather than a new mechanism: the first edit on a read-only project should prompt for which identity is making the change, same as a null-identity Shared-with-you project's first write already does, but then needs an actual write path -- a fork, a PR, a queued-change-for-someone-with-push model -- that doesn't exist yet. Worth scoping once the underlying write-elsewhere mechanism is picked.

history.text: Title set to "remotes[] plural data model for genuine fork/mirror support"
history.value: remotes[] plural data model for genuine fork/mirror support

history.text: Description set to "A project's connection info is currently singular (githubRe…"
history.value: A project's connection info is currently singular (githubRepo/githubRepoPath/githubRepoBranch on the doc, one identityId on the project record). Genuine fork/mirror support -- the same project reachable at two different addresses, or a local copy tracking an upstream it diverged from -- needs a plural remotes[] shape instead, with the existing two-copies-are-the-same-project-when-their-UUIDs-match-not-when-their-addresses-do dedup rule extended to say which remote is home. connectRemoteFinish's existing UUID-match-merges-in behaviour (see tests/connect-remote.spec.js) is the right foundation for this, not a replacement.

history.value: OS-level protocol handler for wigwag: links

history.text: Description set to "The wigwag: URI scheme (project/, remote/, from=/path=/ref=…"
history.value: The wigwag: URI scheme (project/, remote/, from=/path=/ref=) is fully specified and resolves correctly inside the app, but nothing registers wigwag.html as the actual OS handler for wigwag: links clicked outside the app (an email, a Slack message, another tool). Relevant once there's a packaged/installable form of the app to register a handler from -- the Tauri wrapper work is the natural point to pick this up.
